notes.meaning: God calls Zechariah to speak to the Jewish people who had returned home after many years of exile in Babylon. Because Israel no longer had an earthly king of its own, the date is counted by the reign of Darius, the king of Persia. Zechariah begins his ministry just two months after the prophet Haggai to urge the people to rebuild God's temple.

Zechariah reminds his listeners that the Lord had been deeply displeased with their ancestors. The destruction of Jerusalem, the ruins all around them, and the hard years in Babylon were proof of how serious that anger was. Remembering those past troubles was meant to warn the new generation not to make the same mistakes.

God calls His people to turn back to Him from their sins in repentance, which means turning away from wrong ways and heading back to God. In return, God promises to come back to them with His favor, mercy, and peace. The title "LORD of Hosts" is repeated three times to remind them of His supreme power and unlimited strength.

differ.view: The command to turn shows that God gives everyone the ability to choose to return to Him, and no one is lost for lack of power.
The call to turn shows our duty rather than human ability, since fallen people cannot turn to God on their own without the Holy Spirit changing their hearts first.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The command to turn reminds people of their free will, while prayers asking God to turn them admit that God's grace must come first.

notes.meaning: The people are warned not to follow the bad example of their ancestors before the exile. Earlier prophets had pleaded with those ancestors to turn from their evil deeds, but they stubbornly refused to listen to God. Having religious ancestors will not help us if we continue in their sins instead of obeying God.

Both the rebellious ancestors and the prophets who preached to them have died and left the earth. Human life is short, and earthly teachers do not stay around forever. Even though human beings pass away, their deaths should remind us to listen to God's truth while we still have time.

Even though the human preachers died, God's warnings never failed, and they caught up to the people's fathers like an officer arresting a fugitive. In the end, the ancestors had to admit that God had done exactly what He warned He would do. God always keeps His word, which proves that every warning and promise He makes is true.

A few months after his first sermon, Zechariah receives a new series of night visions from the Lord. This happened during the winter month of Shebat, shortly after the people had restarted work on rebuilding God's temple. God gave these revelations to bring fresh hope and direction to the community as they worked.

Zechariah sees a vision in the dark of a rider on a red horse standing among myrtle trees down in a low hollow, with other horses behind him. The lowly myrtle trees in a ravine represent God's people in their humbled, depressed state after the exile. Even when His church is in a low and difficult place, God's heavenly warrior is right there in the middle of them to protect them.

differ.view: The rider among the myrtles is the eternal Son of God appearing in human form as the Angel of the Lord before His birth in Bethlehem.
The rider is a high-ranking created angel leading the patrol, distinct from the Angel of the Lord who appears alongside him.

notes.meaning: Zechariah speaks to an angel who was accompanying him and asks what these strange horses and riders mean. The interpreting angel kindly promises to explain the meaning of the vision. When we do not understand spiritual things, God welcomes our humble desire to be taught.

The rider standing among the myrtles answers the question for the prophet. He explains that the riders are heavenly messengers whom the Lord sent to patrol the entire earth. God constantly watches over the world through His angels to guard His people and manage all earthly events.

The patrol reports back that all the nations of the world are completely quiet, peaceful, and at rest. While the pagan empires enjoyed calm prosperity, God's chosen people were still struggling amid ruins and hardship. It was distressing to see God's enemies sitting comfortably while His own people remained oppressed.

The Angel of the Lord cries out in prayer to the Father, asking how long He will withhold mercy from Jerusalem and Judah. He notes that the seventy years of judgment promised for the exile had already run their full course. This shows the Angel serving as a loving mediator who intercedes, or prays on behalf of, God's hurting people.

The Lord answers the interceding angel with gentle, comforting words of hope for His people. Even though the rebuilding was not yet finished, God spoke real promises that strengthened their faith. God's good words give believers solid assurance that He hears their cries and will act.

The prophet is commanded to proclaim God's deep and passionate love for His people. God describes Himself as "jealous," which means He loves Jerusalem with the fierce, protective care of a faithful husband who will not allow His bride to be harmed. Even after their painful punishment, God's heart was still entirely committed to them.

God declares that He is fiercely angry with the wealthy nations that lived at ease without caring about Israel's pain. While God had used those nations to give His people a measured correction, they went far beyond His purpose and tried to destroy Israel out of sheer cruelty. God will judge anyone who takes pleasure in harming His people.

The Lord promises that He has returned to Jerusalem with tender compassion. His temple will be completely rebuilt, and a builder's measuring line will be stretched out to lay the plan for restoring the entire city. When God returns to His people in mercy, He rebuilds what was once broken down.

Zechariah is told to announce that not only Jerusalem, but all the surrounding towns of Judah will overflow with wealth and people again. The Lord will comfort Zion and openly show that Jerusalem is still His chosen city. God's unfailing love always outlasts our seasons of trial and sorrow.

Zechariah looks up and sees a second vision featuring four animal horns. In the ancient world, animal horns were a well-known picture of earthly power, pride, and military strength. The number four points to enemies that attacked and scattered God's people from every direction.

The interpreting angel explains that these horns represent the fierce world powers that tossed and scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem. These enemy empires had broken up the nation and driven the people from their homeland. Earthly powers may look unstoppable, but God knows every force that tries to harm His people.

The Lord next shows the prophet four craftsmen, or metalworkers, who are equipped with the right tools to break the horns. God makes sure there is a builder or smith ready to deal with each enemy horn. For every enemy that threatens the church, God provides an instrument strong enough to bring it down.

The angel explains that the hostile nations had beaten Judah down so badly that no one could hold their head up. Now, God's craftsmen have come to strike terror into those proud nations and chop their horns to pieces. God always defends His people and will finally shatter every proud power that tries to crush them.
